title: Source verification before Phase 4 (Part 8)
summary: The sources that Research Update 1.1 had only located were looked up again on 12 October 2026, through publisher records, Crossref, Europe PMC and the authors' repositories. Six are now checked, and several citations are completed (DOI, pages) or corrected (a wrong link for LeSuer 1997). No rule's wording, parameters or confidence changes; only evidence records and verification notes do. What could not be read stays listed as pending, with the reason.

approval.by: Delegated: evidence verification only (no wording, parameter or confidence change), reported to the Product Owner at the Phase 3 gate

Bull2020.citation: Bull FC, Al-Ansari SS, Biddle S, et al. World Health Organization 2020 guidelines on physical activity and sedentary behaviour. Br J Sports Med. 2020;54(24):1451-1462. doi:10.1136/bjsports-2020-102955
Bull2020.verification: checked 2026-10-12 (full text, Europe PMC PMC7719906): adults 150-300 min moderate or 75-150 min vigorous a week; muscle strengthening on 2 or more days; adults 65+ varied multicomponent activity emphasising functional balance and strength on 3 or more days

Ding2025.citation: Ding D, Nguyen B, Nau T, et al. Daily steps and health outcomes in adults: a systematic review and dose-response meta-analysis. Lancet Public Health. 2025;10(8):e668-e681. doi:10.1016/S2468-2667(25)00164-1
Ding2025.verification: checked 2026-10-12 (abstract, Baker Institute repository): 7,000 vs 2,000 steps a day, all-cause mortality HR 0.53 (0.46-0.60, moderate certainty), cardiovascular disease incidence HR 0.75, dementia HR 0.62; 10,000 stays a target for more active people; no age-specific analysis

Riebe2015.citation: Riebe D, Franklin BA, Thompson PD, et al. Updating ACSM's recommendations for exercise preparticipation health screening. Med Sci Sports Exerc. 2015;47(11):2473-2479. doi:10.1249/MSS.0000000000000664
Riebe2015.verification: checked 2026-10-12 (abstract, University of Rhode Island repository): screening based on current activity, signs or symptoms and/or known cardiovascular, metabolic or renal disease, and desired intensity; risk-factor profiling dropped

Halperin2022.citation: Halperin I, Malleron T, Har-Nir I, et al. Accuracy in predicting repetitions to task failure in resistance exercise: a scoping review and exploratory meta-analysis. Sports Med. 2022;52(2):377-390. doi:10.1007/s40279-021-01559-x
Halperin2022.verification: checked 2026-10-12 (abstract, Solent University repository): people underpredict repetitions to failure by about 0.95 (95% CI 0.17-1.73), with large heterogeneity; accuracy better with 12 or fewer repetitions and closer to failure; training background made no clear difference

Fragala2019.citation: Fragala MS, Cadore EL, Dorgo S, et al. Resistance training for older adults: position statement from the National Strength and Conditioning Association. J Strength Cond Res. 2019;33(8):2019-2052. doi:10.1519/JSC.0000000000003230
Fragala2019.verification: checked 2026-10-12 (record and abstract, UTEP repository); the program-design recommendations in the full text were not read

LeSuer1997.verification: located; citation checked 2026-10-12 in Crossref (doi:10.1519/00124278-199711000-00001); abstract not read
LeSuer1997.note: The earlier URL opened a different paper (Mayhew et al. 2008, bench press in women).

IDF2006.verification: checked 2026-10-12 through Zimmet PZ, Shaw JE, Alberti KGMM. Mainstreaming the metabolic syndrome: a definitive definition. Med J Aust 2005;183(4):175-176, written by the IDF definition's authors: South Asian and South-East Asian men >= 90 cm, women >= 80 cm; Europid men >= 94 cm, women >= 80 cm. The 2006 IDF document itself was not opened

WHOSTEPS.note: Primary source to read: WHO. Waist circumference and waist-hip ratio: report of a WHO expert consultation, Geneva, 8-11 December 2008. WHO, 2011. ISBN 9789241501491 (record checked 2026-10-12; the report's text could not be opened).

ACOG20.citation: American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists. Physical Activity and Exercise During Pregnancy and the Postpartum Period. Committee Opinion No. 804. Obstet Gynecol. 2020;135(4):e178-e188. doi:10.1097/AOG.0000000000003772
ACOG20.verification: located; citation checked 2026-10-12 in Crossref (pages e178-e188); the full text could not be opened (acog.org and the publisher refused the request)

Donnelly2009.verification: checked 2026-10-12 (abstract, Europe PMC, PMID 19127177): 150-250 min a week of moderate activity gives only modest weight loss; more than 250 min a week is associated with clinically significant loss. The body-text dose bands (225-420 min) were not read; FL-002 does not rely on them

changed_rules.reason: Bull 2020 checked in full text: 150-300 min moderate a week for adults
Bull 2020 checked in full text (2+ strength days; 3+ multicomponent balance and strength days at 65+); Fragala 2019 and Peterson 2011 still to read
the South Asian waist reference lines (90 cm men, 80 cm women) confirmed by the IDF definition's authors; the WHO STEPS protocol text is still to read
Ding 2025 checked (abstract): 7,000 steps a day already brings most of the mortality benefit
Riebe 2015 checked (abstract): activity level, symptoms or known disease, and intended intensity decide the screening

Halperin 2022 checked (abstract): predictions of reps to failure are about one rep low and better at 12 reps or fewer, as the reps + RIR <= 12 limit assumes; LeSuer 1997 citation confirmed, its abstract still to read
